anchor: And the myrtle and ivy of sweet two-and-twenty
note: Myrtle: an evergreen shrub sacred to Venus, goddess of love. Ivy: a clinging evergreen vine.
Laurels: a wreath of laurel leaves, the ancient prize for victors and poets.

anchor: Then away with all such from the head that is hoary
note: Hoary: gray or white with age.

anchor: And the lull’d winds seem dreaming
note: Lull’d: soothed to quiet, made calm and still.

anchor: Meets in her aspect and her eyes
note: Aspect: the look of a face, its expression.

anchor: Thus mellow’d to that tender light
note: Mellow’d: softened and ripened, made gentle in tone.

anchor: Which heaven to gaudy day denies
Had half impair’d the nameless grace
Which waves in every raven tress
note: Raven: glossy black, like the bird. Tress: a lock of hair.
Knell: the sound of a bell rung slowly for a death.
An elegy is a poem of mourning. Thyrza is the name Byron gave the dead woman he mourns.
Disavow: to deny, to refuse to acknowledge.
Lours: frowns, darkens threateningly, as a storm does.
Repine: to complain, to feel discontent.
Vigil: a period of watching or staying awake beside someone.

anchor: Eternal Spirit of the chainless Mind!
note: Chillon is a castle on Lake Geneva. François Bonnivard was imprisoned in its dungeon by the Duke of Savoy for defending his city’s liberty.
source: F. T. Palgrave, The Golden Treasury (1861), Palgrave’s Notes, Poem 209, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/19221

anchor: Worn as if thy cold pavement were a sod, By Bonnivard!
note: Bonnivard was a Genevan who fought the tyranny of Piedmont in the 1500s. Byron says his footsteps wore marks in the dungeon floor.
source: F. T. Palgrave, The Golden Treasury (1861), Palgrave’s Notes, Poem 209, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/19221

anchor: On thee shall press no ponderous tomb
note: Ponderous: heavy and weighty, hard to lift.
